Deep learning
arrives

Three things came together within a few years: a way to train networks with many layers, chips fast enough to run them, and millions of labeled images to learn from. Neural networks stopped being a niche idea and became the front line of AI.

3.1

Layer by layer: deep networks start to work

Chapter 2 ended with a method for training layers of artificial neurons. A network with many layers is called a deep network, and “deep” simply counts the layers the data passes through. Most researchers call a network deep when its depth, the hidden layers plus one for the output, is greater than two.[1] Each layer turns its input into something more abstract. Picture a photo moving upward through the layers, from pixels to edges to shapes to whole objects. That picture is an illustration, but the idea of progressively more abstract representations is the standard description.[1]

In 2006, Geoffrey Hinton, Simon Osindero and Yee-Whye Teh described a way to train such a stack one layer at a time. Each layer first learns from the layer below it, and a final fine-tuning pass refines the whole network.[2] On a standard handwritten-digit test, run without any image-specific tricks, their three-hidden-layer network made 1.25% errors. That beat the roughly 1.5% they cite for the best backpropagation networks of that kind and 1.4% for a support vector machine.[2]

More layers meant more abstraction, and 2006 showed such stacks could be trained well.

Go DeepBack to surface
Deep

How deep is “deep”?

For a network that passes data forward, depth is the number of hidden layers plus one for the output. There is no universal line between shallow and deep.[1]

NetworkHidden layersDepthCalled deep?
Chapter 1’s perceptron01No
One hidden layer12Usually not
The 2006 digit network34Yes

The depth column follows the definition above, and the last row is the network from the 2006 paper.[1][2]

Training one layer at a time

The idea in plain steps: train the first layer on the raw data, freeze it, train the second layer on what the first produces, and so on up the stack. An optional fine-tuning pass with backpropagation can follow.[1][2]

The hardware side was already moving

In 2009, Raina, Madhavan and Ng trained a deep belief network on 30 Nvidia GPUs (the article lists its size as “100M”) and reported training up to 70 times faster.[1] That leads straight into the next section.

Why it matters in education“Deep” is not mysterious. It counts layers. When a product says it uses deep learning, it means a network with several layers of neurons, trained on examples.

Explainers

From section 3.1Deep learning

Deep learning is a class of machine learning methods that uses multilayered neural networks to turn input data into increasingly abstract representations, for tasks such as classification and regression.[1]

YearStep
1986Backpropagation is popularized (Chapter 2)
2006Layer-by-layer training of deep belief networks
2009A large network is trained on 30 GPUs, up to 70 times faster
2012AlexNet wins the ImageNet competition

By 2019, GPUs had displaced CPUs as the dominant way to train large commercial AI systems in the cloud.[1]

3.2

GPUs change the speed limit

A graphics processing unit, or GPU, was built to draw images. Drawing a screen means doing the same simple calculation for thousands of pixels, mostly independent of each other. A modern GPU holds hundreds or thousands of small calculation units working side by side.[3] Training a neural network turns out to be the same kind of job: enormous numbers of simple multiplications. GPUs accelerate exactly the arithmetic that neural network training depends on.[3]

In 2007, Nvidia’s CUDA made GPUs practical to program for general tasks, and it became the first widely adopted way to do so.[3] By 2019, GPUs had displaced ordinary processors as the dominant way to train large commercial AI.[1]

The breakthrough was less a smarter idea than many more hands working at once.

500
Strong team

What the demo shows

When jobs do not depend on each other, adding workers shortens the time almost without limit. When each job needs the previous result, extra workers sit idle and only the speed of a single worker counts. Computer scientists call the first kind embarrassingly parallel, the term the GPU article uses for problems where the same simple operation runs on many items at once.[3]

From graphics to AI

The modern GPU emerged in the 1990s. ATI’s Radeon 9700 (2002) added shaders that could loop and do long floating-point calculations, and Nvidia’s GeForce 8 series made the chips more general-purpose. Researchers soon used them for linear algebra and statistics, and CUDA followed in 2007.[3]

Why it matters in educationWhen people say AI needs huge data centers, this is the reason. The work is a vast pile of simple, independent calculations, and the more hands the better.

Explainers

From section 3.2GPU

A GPU is a specialized electronic circuit built to accelerate computer graphics and image processing. It can be a separate card or built into a phone, PC or game console, and it is also used to process and train AI models.[3]

3.3

ImageNet and AlexNet (2012)

Deep networks also needed data, and ImageNet supplied it. Starting in 2006, the researcher Fei-Fei Li built a database of more than 14 million labeled images in over 20,000 categories.[4] The labeling was crowdsourced: about 49,000 workers from 167 countries sorted more than 160 million candidate images.[4] From 2010, an annual contest asked programs to sort images into 1,000 categories.[4]

In 2012, a team at the University of Toronto, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton, entered a deep convolutional network called AlexNet. Its top-5 error rate was 15.3%, which means the right answer was usually among its first five guesses. That beat the runner-up by more than 10 percentage points.[5] It was the same family as Chapter 2’s LeNet, but with eight layers and about 60 million parameters, trained for five to six days on two Nvidia GTX 580 GPUs that cost about US$500 each.[5]

Method, data and hardware arrived together. 2012 was the moment it showed.

Why it was a turning point

AlexNet is regarded as the first widely recognized large-scale use of deep convolutional networks for visual recognition. Yann LeCun called it “an unequivocal turning point in the history of computer vision.”[5] The network did not fit on a single GPU’s 3 GB of memory, so it was split across two.[5]

Why it matters in educationNo single invention caused 2012. The method existed, the data had been assembled, and the hardware was affordable. That is a useful way to explain why AI seemed to arrive suddenly.

Explainers

From section 3.3Overfitting and underfitting

Overfitting is when a model learns its training data too closely, noise included, so it does poorly on new data. The sign is low error on training data but high error on held-out test data.[11]

Underfitting is the opposite: the model has not trained long enough or lacks informative inputs, so it misses the main trend and generalizes poorly to new data.[11] The table below is my own summary.

UnderfitGood fitOverfit
Training errorHighLowVery low
New-data errorHighLowHigh

A model with 60 million parameters, like AlexNet, has plenty of room to memorize (my own point). Causes of overfitting include training too long and a model that is too complex for the problem, and common remedies are early stopping, more training data and regularization.[11] AlexNet itself used techniques such as dropout and data augmentation.[5]

3.4

Watson, Siri, and learning without labels

Two products made AI visible to the public in 2011. In February, IBM’s Watson beat Jeopardy!’s best-known champions, Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter, finishing with $77,147 to their $24,000 and $21,600.[6][7] Watson was not one deep network. IBM said it combined more than 100 different techniques, and its question-answering system did not use deep neural networks.[6] In October, Apple shipped Siri on the iPhone 4S, a voice assistant that began as a spin-off from SRI International’s AI lab. Its speech recognition uses machine learning, including convolutional and LSTM networks.[8]

Everything so far in this chapter learned from labeled examples, and labels are expensive: ImageNet needed tens of thousands of workers.[4] Unsupervised learning skips the labels. The model gets raw data and finds structure by itself, based on similarities, differences and patterns.[9]

Supervised learning needs an answer key. Unsupervised learning has to find the pattern without one.

What happened to Watson

Watson’s first commercial application was announced in 2013, in cancer treatment decisions at Memorial Sloan Kettering. From 2012 into the late 2010s it was tried in cancer care, retail, cooking, weather and tax preparation, and most of those uses were later discontinued. IBM divested its Watson Health division in 2022, and it was sold to Francisco Partners for about $1 billion, after about $4 billion had been spent developing it.[6] On the show itself, Watson answered “Toronto” to a U.S. Cities clue in Final Jeopardy.[6][7]

Why it matters in educationWatson is a reminder that a spectacular demo and a useful product are different things. It also helps separate “AI” from “deep learning”: Watson was AI, but mostly not deep learning.

Explainers

Unsupervised learning finds patterns in data without labels or human-provided answers. The model infers its own structure from similarities and differences.[9]

3.5

GANs and deepfakes (2014)

In June 2014, Ian Goodfellow and colleagues at the Université de Montréal proposed training two networks against each other.[12][13] One, the generator, makes fake samples such as images. The other, the discriminator, judges whether each sample is real or fake. The generator improves by learning to fool the judge, and the judge improves by learning to catch the fakes.[12][13] The result is a generative adversarial network, or GAN.

A forger and a detective, each forcing the other to get better.

GANs produced strikingly realistic images, and they became a key turning point for deepfakes,[14] a word blending “deep learning” and “fake.” The term arose in late 2017 on Reddit, where users posted face-swapped videos.[14] GANs also have constructive uses, such as synthetic medical images and art. In 2018 a GAN-made painting sold for US$432,500.[12]

Solid line: real data. Dashed line: the forger’s fakes. At 50% the detective is guessing, and the fakes match the real data.

The theory in one line

The original paper shows that, in theory, the game has a solution where the generator reproduces the real data and the discriminator outputs one half everywhere, meaning it cannot tell the difference. When both networks are multilayer perceptrons, they can be trained with backpropagation.[13]

Known weaknesses

Two well-known problems are mode collapse, where the generator produces only a narrow slice of what it could, and unstable training.[12]

Deepfakes and detection

Early deepfakes used autoencoders, networks that compress and rebuild images. GANs, which pit a generator against a discriminator, were a key turning point in the mid-2010s and became the basis for modern methods.[14] Detection is a constant race. The winning model in the Deepfake Detection Challenge was 65% accurate on its holdout set, and an MIT study found ordinary people were 69 to 72% accurate on a sample of 50 videos.[14]

Documented harms include fraud (a 2024 case cost the firm Arup $25 million), non-consensual pornography (a 2019 report estimated 96% of online deepfakes were pornographic) and political disinformation. Researchers also warn of a “liar’s dividend,” where real recordings can be dismissed as fakes.[14]

Why it matters in educationSeeing is no longer proof. Teaching students to check the source and context of an image or video will age better than teaching them to spot telltale flaws, because the flaws keep disappearing.

Explainers

From section 3.5GAN

A generative adversarial network trains two networks together as a game. The generator tries to produce samples that look real, and the discriminator tries to tell real from generated.[12][13]

PartJobAnalogy
GeneratorMake convincing fakes from random inputThe forger
DiscriminatorJudge real versus fakeThe detective

GANs were first proposed for unsupervised learning.[12] The analogy column is mine, for orientation.

3.6

AlphaGo and AlphaFold

Chapter 2 ended with Deep Blue beating a chess champion using hand-built rules and brute force. Go is a far harder game for computers, and experts had expected a program this strong to be at least five years away.[15] In October 2015, DeepMind’s AlphaGo beat the European champion Fan Hui 5 to 0. In March 2016 in Seoul, it beat the 9-dan player Lee Sedol 4 to 1.[15]

What changed is how it learned. AlphaGo first trained on about 30 million moves from recorded expert games, then played large numbers of games against copies of itself and improved through reinforcement learning, learning from wins and losses.[15] Deep Blue’s knowledge of chess was written by people. AlphaGo’s came from data and practice.

Deep Blue was told how to judge a position. AlphaGo learned how.

The same approach moved into science. AlphaFold predicts a protein’s 3D shape from its sequence of amino acids. Experiments had worked out about 170,000 structures over 60 years, while more than 200 million proteins are known.[16] AlphaFold came first at the 2018 contest, and in 2020 its second version made the best prediction for 88 of 97 targets.[16] Its creators Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared half of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.[16] AlphaFold falls after 2016, but it belongs to the same story.

How AlphaGo was put together

It used two convolutional networks, one to suggest moves (a policy network) and one to judge positions (a value network). They guided a search over possible continuations of the game.[15] The convolutional network is the same kind of network as Chapter 2’s LeNet.

A human moment

Lee Sedol won Game 4, the only game he took. His move 78 in that game, nicknamed the “divine move,” exposed a weakness that AlphaGo could not adjust to during that game. The team later said it had been patched.[15]

Why protein shapes matter

A protein’s 3-D structure is necessary to understand its biological function, and experimental methods to find shapes are costly and slow. In 2021, DeepMind and the European Bioinformatics Institute launched an openly licensed database of predicted structures. By late July 2022 it held structures for around 200 million proteins.[16] The source adds that the broader protein-folding problem remains unsolved, despite the progress.[16]

Why it matters in educationThis is where learning clearly beats hand-written rules: situations too rich for anyone to write down all the knowledge. Games were the test bed, and science is the payoff.

Explainers

From section 3.6Reinforcement learning

Reinforcement learning is a type of machine learning in which an agent learns good behavior by interacting with an environment through trial and error, receiving rewards or penalties.[10]

  1. Observe. The agent looks at the current state of its environment.
  2. Act. Following its policy, its current strategy, it picks an action.
  3. Get feedback. The environment changes and the agent receives a reward.
  4. Update. The agent adjusts its policy to favor actions that led to rewards.[10]

The goal is to maximize reward over time. In a chess example, the actions are moves, the environment is the board and the reward is winning.[10] The balance between trying new things and repeating what works, shown in the demo above, is a standard idea in the field (my note, not from the cited page).
